headline: Race Point Ebb: Stripers to 30 on Live Mackerel, Haddock Holding at Peaked Hill
subhead: Cooler Bay water is keeping the bass honest through daylight while cod and haddock settle into the deeper rips off Provincetown.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had the boat idling off Race Point with the tide starting to slack out of the ebb, and the water in front of me just dimpled — mackerel, thousands of them, working bait up against the rip line. I don't chase that kind of thing anymore, I just shut down and let it come to me. Fifteen minutes with small diamond jigs and I had a livewell full of mackerel, the kind of bait that turns a slow morning into a good one. By eight o'clock I had three rods bent with bass in the 20 to 30 pound range, all on those live mackerel drifted just off the bottom in about 25 feet of water, right where the rip meets the sandy gut off the Race. One fish, a low-30, came off after a solid ten minutes of give and take — that's the Bay in July, you win some and you lose some, and you don't get mad about it.

That's been the story most mornings this week. The rest of the coast is dealing with warm, sleepy water that's pushed the bass into feeding only at night, but Cape Cod Bay doesn't play by those rules. This water stays cooler than the south side of the Cape and it keeps stripers willing to eat through the middle of the day, especially right on the rips where current stacks bait against structure. Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars have both been holding fish through the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood — that's your window, roughly a three-hour stretch where the current is still moving enough to hold bait tight but hasn't gone slack yet. Once it goes dead slack, the bite usually dies with it, and you're better off running to check structure than sitting there soaking a bait in flat water.

Bluefish have been mixed into that same water, chopping up mackerel schools on the surface some mornings, which is a mess to fish through if you're trying to keep bass baits intact, but it's better than not having bait around at all. We flagged last week that bluefish would keep following the bunker and bait pods up the coast, and that's exactly what's playing out here — you'll see blues show up in the same rips as the bass, sometimes in the same five-minute window, so don't be surprised if you're re-rigging a lot.

Out deeper, Peaked Hill Bars and the rock piles off Provincetown Harbor have been holding cod and haddock steady in that 60 to 90 foot range. Nothing spectacular in size — mostly 17-inch to maybe 6-pound fish — but it's a dependable meal if the bass bite goes quiet on you. Jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of squid, or drifting clams on a simple two-hook bottom rig, has been the play. You want to be right on the structure, not off to the side of it — these fish are hugging the rock and you'll feel the difference in a hurry when your jig ticks bottom right instead of just dragging over sand.

Billingsgate has been the fluke spot this week, and it's been solid, not spectacular — a few keepers in the 18 to 22 inch range mixed with a lot of shorts on white Gulp Swimming Mullets fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow across the sand-to-mud transition on the last of the incoming tide. That's typical Billingsgate — the fluke sit right where the bottom changes character, and if you're not paying attention to your chart you'll drift right past the good stretch without knowing it. Sandy Neck has had some bluefish action working the beach as bait pushes along the shoreline, mostly smaller blues in the 2 to 4 pound range, fun on light tackle but nothing to write home about size-wise.

We're coming up on the first-quarter neap later this week, and that's going to soften the current through the rips for a few days. That's usually a mixed blessing out here — it widens the window where you can fish productively because the tide isn't ripping through as hard, but it also spreads the bait out more, so you spend more time hunting and less time just anchoring up on a known spot. If I had one day to fish this weekend, I'd still start at Race Point on that last two hours of ebb, because that structure holds bait even when the current isn't screaming, and I'd have a backup plan to run out to Peaked Hill if the bass don't show inside the first hour.

Mackerel have been thick enough this week that livelining is the easy call over eels or bucktails, and I'd keep it that way as long as they're showing up on the fishfinder in that same tight window off the Race. If the mackerel schools move or thin out, that's when I'll switch back to swimming plugs and bucktails worked slow along the rip edges. For now, the pattern's holding — cooler water, daylight bass, dependable bottom fish deeper down. Not a blow-out week, but a solid one, and out here this time of year, solid is plenty.
